raw_evidence.content: The English Reformation under Henry VIII reshaped Oxford between roughly 1536 and 1546. Monastic colleges that served religious orders were dissolved: Gloucester College and others were suppressed in 1539, and St Mary's College and St Bernard's College fell in 1540, ceasing to function after the dissolution of the monasteries cut off the clergy who staffed them. At the same time, new foundations rose from the wreckage. Thomas Wolsey's Cardinal College (1525) was suppressed when Wolsey fell, refounded as King Henry VIII's College in 1532, and finally re-established by the king in 1546 as Christ Church — simultaneously the cathedral of the new Diocese of Oxford. This churn explains why the 16th century is the single biggest century in the dataset by foundations: it is partly a story of destruction and renaming, not pure growth.

raw_evidence.label: 1879 and the women's colleges
raw_evidence.content: The 19th-century expansion in the dataset is partly the arrival of women at Oxford. Lady Margaret Hall, founded in 1878, was the first women's college and admitted its first nine students in 1879; the non-denominational Somerville Hall opened the same year, the two splitting over religious lines. St Anne's, St Hugh's (1886) and St Hilda's (1893) followed. Crucially, these institutions existed for decades before women could actually take Oxford degrees: women attended lectures and sat exams but were not full members of the University until 1920, when the first women had MA degrees conferred. The dataset's 19th-century cluster therefore marks not just numerical growth but a structural change in who Oxford was for.

Green Templeton (2008) is the product of a merger — Green College (1979) joined Templeton College (1965), the first such merger in the university's modern history, which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear in the dataset. Kellogg, Reuben and St Cross are 'societies' without a royal charter rather than full chartered colleges.

Namesakes split between the religious (Mary Magdalene, John the Baptist, All Souls' Day, the Holy Trinity, Jesus Christ) and the personal (the founder themselves, royal consorts like Philippa of Hainault, scholars like Mary Somerville and Thomas Linacre). This makes the dataset a compact social history of who held wealth and power in England across eight centuries — from the medieval Church, through the Crown, to 20th-century industry and finance. A reader can trace the secularisation of patronage straight through the 'named_after' column.

raw_evidence.label: The modern graduate-college wave and Reuben (2019)
raw_evidence.content: The 20th and 21st century foundations in the dataset are dominated by graduate colleges, often endowed by industrial philanthropists: Nuffield (1937, motor magnate Lord Nuffield), Wolfson (1965, Isaac Wolfson), Kellogg (1990, the cereal foundation), and Reuben (2019). Reuben College is the newest, the first new Oxford college since Kellogg in 1990; it was established graduate-only in 2019, took its name after an £80 million gift from the Reuben Foundation in 2020, and enrolled its first students in 2021 in the former Radcliffe Science Library. Green Templeton (2008) is the product of a merger — Green College (1979) joined Templeton College (1965), the first such merger in the university's modern history, which is why both Templeton and Green Templeton appear in the dataset. Kellogg, Reuben and St Cross are 'societies' without a royal charter rather than full chartered colleges.
